claims.claim: Vitiligo is a chronic condition with pigment loss caused by loss of working melanocytes, the cells that make melanin.
In common non-segmental vitiligo the immune system attacks melanocytes; white patches often appear on both sides, including hands and face.
Hair in affected areas can turn white; extent and progression vary.
Vitiligo is not an infection and is not contagious.
Family history and other autoimmune conditions can be associated with vitiligo.
Diagnosis uses skin examination; a Wood lamp can help distinguish pigment loss, and selected patients may need thyroid testing.
Affected skin is vulnerable to sunburn; high-SPF sunscreen and sun protection are important.
Treatment can include clinician-supervised topical medicines; camouflage is optional. Response varies and no cure is guaranteed. Support for emotional impact can help.
New pale patches should be assessed rather than self-diagnosed.

claims.claim: The urinary tract includes two kidneys, two ureters, a bladder and a urethra; kidneys produce urine, ureters carry it to the bladder, the bladder stores it, and the urethra carries it outside.
Bacteria, usually from the bowel, can enter through the urethra and multiply in the bladder; an untreated bladder infection can develop into a kidney infection.
Burning urination, urgency, frequency, lower abdominal discomfort and sometimes blood in urine are symptoms; smell or dark urine alone does not establish UTI.
Catheters, impaired bladder emptying, pregnancy and menopause can increase risk.
Clinical assessment uses symptoms and history and may include urine testing; urine testing is not always needed.

Antibiotics are often used for bacterial bladder infection; take prescribed treatment as directed. Rest and appropriate fluids may help symptoms, but cranberry products do not treat an established infection.
Fever or chills, back pain below the ribs, blood in urine, pregnancy, or rapid worsening warrant urgent medical advice; new confusion, marked drowsiness or difficulty speaking warrant emergency help.
Not holding urine, taking time to empty the bladder and drinking appropriate fluids may help urinary health; follow clinician fluid limits when applicable.

claims.claim: Multiple sclerosis is an immune-mediated disorder affecting the central nervous system: brain and spinal cord; immune attacks damage myelin around axons and may damage axons themselves, disrupting communication.
Myelin is the protective coating around nerve fibers; demyelinated lesions can occur in the brain and spinal cord and can be seen with MRI.
Symptoms vary by person and lesion location: fatigue, visual problems, numbness or tingling, muscle weakness or stiffness, and balance problems can occur.
Some people have relapses and remissions; others experience progressive worsening. The course varies and cannot be predicted from a single illustration.

The exact cause is unclear; genetic susceptibility and environmental factors contribute, and smoking and prior Epstein-Barr virus infection are associated with increased risk, not certainty of disease.
No single test diagnoses MS: a neurologist combines history and examination with MRI and sometimes spinal fluid or other tests, excluding other causes.
There is no current cure. Disease-modifying therapies can reduce relapses and slow progression for appropriate patients; treatment depends on disease type and individual needs.
Corticosteroids may speed recovery from a relapse but do not change the long-term course; physiotherapy, tailored exercise, fatigue management and symptom medicines can help.
Sudden arm weakness or numbness, sudden vision loss or sudden balance problems can signal stroke and require emergency medical help; do not assume they are MS.
MS-like symptoms can have other causes and should be checked by a clinician; general education is not diagnosis.

claims.claim: The pancreas lies behind the stomach near the duodenum; it makes insulin and digestive enzymes that normally help digest food in the intestine.
Acute pancreatitis is sudden inflammation of the pancreas; digestive enzymes can damage pancreatic tissue.
Gallstones can block the opening of the pancreas; gallstones and heavy alcohol use are common causes, while some medicines and other conditions can also cause it.
Symptoms include sudden persistent severe upper abdominal pain that may spread to the back, nausea, vomiting and fever.
Sudden severe persistent abdominal pain needs urgent medical evaluation; severe pain spreading to the back, fast heartbeat or difficulty breathing warrants emergency care.
Evaluation uses history, examination, blood tests and sometimes imaging such as CT.
Hospital treatment includes monitoring, IV fluids and pain relief; treating the cause may include gallstone surgery or alcohol cessation support. Antibiotics are for infection, not a routine cure.
Most people recover, but severe illness may cause tissue death or infection and can be life-threatening.
Reducing or avoiding alcohol, stopping smoking and following clinician dietary advice may help prevent recurrence.

claims.claim: Milky seas are rare expanses of steady whitish marine bioluminescence visible at night.
Luminous bacteria are implicated, but their precise ecological relationships and conditions producing milky seas remain uncertain.
At high bacterial population density, chemical quorum sensing can trigger bacterial luminescence.
A 1985 sampled milky sea contained luminous bacteria associated with microalgae.
The glow may persist for days to weeks and drift with surface currents.
The VIIRS day-night band can detect the faint glow from orbit under favorable conditions; moonlight and clouds can complicate detection.
Unlike a milky sea’s steady glow, mechanically stimulated dinoflagellate bioluminescence typically flashes briefly.

claims.claim: Chrysoperla rufilabris is a green lacewing found in North America; humid habitats include irrigated crops and greenhouses.
Adults are pale green, with golden eyes, long antennae and transparent wings; adult size is roughly 12–20 mm.
Eggs are laid singly on silken stalks on foliage.
Larvae have three instars, legs and large curved paired mouthparts; they impale aphids and suck body contents.
Mature larvae spin a round silken cocoon; the pupa develops before the adult emerges.
Chrysoperla adults feed on nectar, pollen and honeydew while larvae are predators.
Generalized insect body plan: spiracles admit air into branching tracheae; the alimentary canal carries food and the ventral nerve cord runs along the body.
